papers.title: Quantifying the extinction probability of Marburg virus disease outbreaks: A continuous-time Markov chain model integrating a multi-type branching process
papers.abstract: Understanding the extinction dynamics of Marburg virus disease is crucial, particularly during the early stages of an outbreak when stochastic effects strongly influence disease outcomes. Although deterministic models have provided valuable insights into virus transmission dynamics, they cannot adequately capture random transmission events or quantify extinction probabilities, particularly when outbreaks begin with few infected cases. This study develops a continuous-time Markov chain stochastic model derived from a deterministic multi-host transmission model. The model incorporates a multi-type branching process, in which distinct infectious types are tracked according to their contributions to secondary infections, enabling estimation of disease extinction probabilities during the early outbreak phase. The extinction analysis shows that outbreaks initiated by exposed humans have a higher probability of extinction (21.6%) compared with those initiated by infectious humans (13.7%), whereas outbreaks initiated by infected bats have an extinction probability of only 0.36%, highlighting their role as important reservoirs sustaining virus transmission. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that reducing human-to-human transmission, decreasing viral shedding, and increasing environmental viral decay significantly enhance the likelihood of disease extinction. The proposed framework provides a quantitative tool for assessing Marburg virus disease outbreak risk and valuable insights for designing early interventions for human transmission, environmental contamination, and cross-species interactions.

papers.source_body_en: Understanding the extinction dynamics of Marburg virus disease is crucial, particularly during the early stages of an outbreak when stochastic effects strongly influence disease outcomes. Although deterministic models have provided valuable insights into virus transmission dynamics, they cannot adequately capture random transmission events or quantify extinction probabilities, particularly when outbreaks begin with few infected cases. This study develops a continuous-time Markov chain stochastic model derived from a deterministic multi-host transmission model. The model incorporates a multi-type branching process, in which distinct infectious types are tracked according to their contributions to secondary infections, enabling estimation of disease extinction probabilities during the early outbreak phase. The extinction analysis shows that outbreaks initiated by exposed humans have a higher probability of extinction (21.6%) compared with those initiated by infectious humans (13.7%), whereas outbreaks initiated by infected bats have an extinction probability of only 0.36%, highlighting their role as important reservoirs sustaining virus transmission. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that reducing human-to-human transmission, decreasing viral shedding, and increasing environmental viral decay significantly enhance the likelihood of disease extinction. The proposed framework provides a quantitative tool for assessing Marburg virus disease outbreak risk and valuable insights for designing early interventions for human transmission, environmental contamination, and cross-species interactions.

papers.abstract: A critical, annotated version of Narlikar’s iconic novel about a cybervirus attack by an advanced alien species—with updated text and added material. A year before Robin Cook’s Invasion (1997)—in which an alien force activates a latent biological virus in humans—and almost a decade before Liu Cixin’s The Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy (2008–2010)—in which humanity’s scientific progress is curtailed by an alien supercomputer’s “sophon-lock”—Jayant Vishnu Narlikar’s Virus (1996) painted a similar scenario. In his novel, a cybervirus broadcast by an advanced, extraterrestrial species invades Earth and freezes its digital infrastructure: a prelude to an alien invasion. The novel, first published in Marathi, recounts how vast radio arrays on Earth intercept a seemingly innocuous message from an unknown planet orbiting Barnard’s Star. The radio signal, sent six years prior, coalesces into a cybervirus that has the potential to cause a complete digital meltdown and lead humanity into an age of chaos—an alien first strike to prevent humanity from evolving further. This book—a critical, annotated version of Virus, edited and revised by Sami Ahmad Khan—reissues Narlikar’s iconic novel with updated text and added dimensions. It includes detailed annotations that locate the technology of the text along the axis of contemporary scientific thought, as well as critical essays that focus on the literary, political, and sociocultural dimensions of the novel; essays on Narlikar’s role in India’s science and science fiction; an exclusive conversation with the author; bibliographical information on his works; and a bonus short story. Contributions by Sami Ahmad Khan, Nilam Ingole, Priteegandha Naik, Jayant V. Narlikar, and Dibyadyuti Roy.

papers.source_body_en: A critical, annotated version of Narlikar’s iconic novel about a cybervirus attack by an advanced alien species—with updated text and added material. A year before Robin Cook’s Invasion (1997)—in which an alien force activates a latent biological virus in humans—and almost a decade before Liu Cixin’s The Remembrance of Earth’s Past trilogy (2008–2010)—in which humanity’s scientific progress is curtailed by an alien supercomputer’s “sophon-lock”—Jayant Vishnu Narlikar’s Virus (1996) painted a similar scenario. In his novel, a cybervirus broadcast by an advanced, extraterrestrial species invades Earth and freezes its digital infrastructure: a prelude to an alien invasion. The novel, first published in Marathi, recounts how vast radio arrays on Earth intercept a seemingly innocuous message from an unknown planet orbiting Barnard’s Star. The radio signal, sent six years prior, coalesces into a cybervirus that has the potential to cause a complete digital meltdown and lead humanity into an age of chaos—an alien first strike to prevent humanity from evolving further. This book—a critical, annotated version of Virus, edited and revised by Sami Ahmad Khan—reissues Narlikar’s iconic novel with updated text and added dimensions. It includes detailed annotations that locate the technology of the text along the axis of contemporary scientific thought, as well as critical essays that focus on the literary, political, and sociocultural dimensions of the novel; essays on Narlikar’s role in India’s science and science fiction; an exclusive conversation with the author; bibliographical information on his works; and a bonus short story. Contributions by Sami Ahmad Khan, Nilam Ingole, Priteegandha Naik, Jayant V. Narlikar, and Dibyadyuti Roy.

papers.title: Beyond Viral Pathogenesis: Climate Change, Zoonotic Spillover, and the Evolving Epidemiology of Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers
papers.abstract: Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) represent a major global health threat because they can cause severe systemic illness, hemorrhage, multiorgan dysfunction, and death. Ebola virus, Marburg virus, Lassa virus, and Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever virus contribute substantially to the global burden of these diseases. These pathogens employ diverse transmission routes, including vector-borne transmission, zoonotic spillover, and direct exposure to infected bodily fluids. Climate change, land use alterations, urbanization, population growth, and increased human–animal interactions may reshape pathogen ecology and create new opportunities for viral emergence and transmission. International travel and interconnected human populations further complicate outbreak containment. This review examines the pathophysiological mechanisms, epidemiological patterns, and major outbreaks associated with VHFs, with particular emphasis on how environmental change, ecological disruption, and infectious disease dynamics interact. We also evaluate the roles of global health organizations in strengthening disease surveillance, coordinating outbreak responses, and promoting international preparedness. Furthermore, we discuss the importance of integrated surveillance systems, cross-sectoral collaboration, and climate-informed public health strategies in reducing the risks associated with emerging and recurring VHF outbreaks. By integrating virological, ecological, epidemiological, and public health perspectives, this review highlights critical knowledge gaps and identifies priorities for improving early detection, outbreak preparedness, and coordinated responses to future VHF threats.

papers.source_body_en: Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) represent a major global health threat because they can cause severe systemic illness, hemorrhage, multiorgan dysfunction, and death. Ebola virus, Marburg virus, Lassa virus, and Crimean–Congo hemorrhagic fever virus contribute substantially to the global burden of these diseases. These pathogens employ diverse transmission routes, including vector-borne transmission, zoonotic spillover, and direct exposure to infected bodily fluids. Climate change, land use alterations, urbanization, population growth, and increased human–animal interactions may reshape pathogen ecology and create new opportunities for viral emergence and transmission. International travel and interconnected human populations further complicate outbreak containment. This review examines the pathophysiological mechanisms, epidemiological patterns, and major outbreaks associated with VHFs, with particular emphasis on how environmental change, ecological disruption, and infectious disease dynamics interact. We also evaluate the roles of global health organizations in strengthening disease surveillance, coordinating outbreak responses, and promoting international preparedness. Furthermore, we discuss the importance of integrated surveillance systems, cross-sectoral collaboration, and climate-informed public health strategies in reducing the risks associated with emerging and recurring VHF outbreaks. By integrating virological, ecological, epidemiological, and public health perspectives, this review highlights critical knowledge gaps and identifies priorities for improving early detection, outbreak preparedness, and coordinated responses to future VHF threats.

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA South Sudan + 1 more South Sudan MVD Readiness - DREF Final Report (MDRSS018) Format Situation Report Source IFRC Posted 18 Nov 2026 Originally published 17 Nov 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 1.27 MB) Description of the Event Date when the trigger was met 23-12-2025 What happened, where and when? The Marburg Virus Disease (MVD) outbreak was declared in Ethiopia on 14 November 2025, prompting heightened preparedness measures in neighboring South Sudan due to the risk of cross-border transmission through frequent population movement, trade, and pastoral migration. On 23 December 2025, three suspected MVD-related deaths were reported in Kapoeta East County, including two individuals with a recent travel history to the affected areas of Ethiopia and one suspected community-linked case. These alerts triggered increased preparedness and readiness efforts by the South Sudan Red Cross (SSRC) in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and partners. The operation was implemented from 30 December 2025 to 28 February 2026 in the high-risk border counties of Akobo, Maiwut, Pibor, and Kapoeta East, which had been identified as priority locations because of their proximity to Ethiopia and high levels of cross-border movement. Preparedness activities included volunteer training, community-based surveillance, risk communication and community engagement (RCCE), infection prevention and control (IPC), hygiene promotion, and Safe and Dignified Burial (SDB) preparedness. During implementation, the epidemiological situation remained stable and no confirmed MVD cases were reported in South Sudan. Investigations into suspected alerts, including those reported in Kapoeta East, did not result in any confirmed Marburg cases, and one suspected alert investigated during the operation tested negative. However, operational challenges affected implementation. In Akobo and Maiwut, insecurity and localized conflict restricted access to some communities and required volunteers and staff to relocate temporarily to safer locations while continuing awareness activities where feasible. In Pibor, cattle-raiding incidents disrupted planned interventions and limited access to some target areas. In Kapoeta East, poor road conditions and the remoteness of border communities presented logistical challenges, although SSRC successfully reached border locations, trained volunteers, and implemented preparedness activities. By the end of the operation, no confirmed MVD cases had been detected in South Sudan. The outbreak situation in Ethiopia had improved, transmission had been brought under control, and preparedness capacities in the targeted counties had been strengthened through trained volunteers, community awareness, surveillance systems, IPC measures, and SDB readiness mechanisms. The findings, published in the International Journal of Emergency Medicine, examine patients treated at the Jinka General Hospital Marburg Virus Disease Treatment Center during an outbreak declared by the Ethiopian Ministry of Health in late October 2025. Across the entire outbreak response, public health surveillance identified 19 total cases, comprising 14 laboratory-confirmed infections and five probable cases. Among the 14 confirmed cases, nine individuals died, reflecting an overall case fatality rate of 64.3 percent, while five survived following intensive inpatient management. Marburg virus disease is a severe, often lethal hemorrhagic fever caused by Marburg virus, a member of the Filoviridae family first identified in 1967 after simultaneous outbreaks in Marburg and Frankfurt, Germany, and Belgrade, Yugoslavia, linked to laboratory work with African green monkeys imported from Uganda. The pathogen maintains a natural wildlife reservoir in the Egyptian fruit bat, and human infections carry historical case fatality rates ranging between 24 percent and 90 percent depending on the specific viral strain, host factors, and local clinical capabilities. Clinically, the infection typically begins with an abrupt, nonspecific febrile illness characterized by high fever, severe headache, chills, and profound fatigue, before progressing rapidly to severe gastrointestinal manifestations such as intractable vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and intense abdominal pain. Advanced stages frequently involve coagulation abnormalities, marked vascular permeability, and overt bleeding, which can precipitate multi-organ failure, circulatory collapse, and shock. The five survivors detailed in the report included four females and one male with a median age of 18 years, who were admitted and managed between November and December 2025. Epidemiological evaluations revealed that four of the cases arose through identifiable transmission chains within community and occupational settings. Three patients were household contacts of known probable or confirmed Marburg cases, including one individual whose father was a probable case and whose uncle died of confirmed disease, and another patient who provided extensive caregiver support to two infected siblings who both died. A fourth patient was a 32-year-old female healthcare worker stationed at the Jinka treatment center who had direct occupational contact with confirmed patients over a two-week period and later served in pre-triage care, where she assisted during the delivery-related care of an infected woman despite wearing personal protective equipment. Discover more Study Biology Check Symptoms Save on Rx Book Care Services Read Med Journals Upon hospital admission, all five patients exhibited classic initial clinical manifestations of filovirus infection, presenting uniformly with fever, generalized headache, fatigue, and gastrointestinal complaints. Hematological and biochemical evaluations across the cohort demonstrated classic hallmarks of systemic filoviral illness, including profound bone marrow suppression and direct hepatocellular injury. Marked leukopenia was documented across the cohort, reaching a nadir white blood cell count of 1.55 times 10 to the third power cells per microliter, accompanied by severe thrombocytopenia with a platelet nadir of 65 times 10 to the third power cells per microliter. Hepatic involvement was universally evident through elevated transaminases, reaching an extreme peak aspartate aminotransferase level of 1,153 units per liter in one severely affected patient. Additionally, one patient experienced profound neutropenia, with an absolute neutrophil count dropping to 107 cells per microliter. Overt hemorrhagic complications developed in three of the five survivors between the fifth and seventh days after symptom onset, a timeline that mirrors the progression seen in previous Central and East African outbreaks. The first patient, a 15-year-old female who presented five days after contact with a suspected fatal case, suffered three episodes of hematemesis alongside high fever, cough, abdominal pain, and scattered erythematous maculopapular skin lesions. Another patient, an 18-year-old female admitted shortly after the death of a suspected household contact, quickly progressed into the hemorrhagic phase, experiencing significant upper gastrointestinal bleeding with baseline hemoglobin measurements fluctuating between 11.6 and 14.6 grams per deciliter. A 35-year-old female caregiver similarly presented with bloody diarrhea and a history of upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, followed by a critical phase around day five marked by persistent fever reaching 39.5 degrees Celsius and severe hepatic injury. Discover more Track Outbreaks Find Treatments infection Therapeutic management for all five surviving patients integrated experimental antiviral therapy alongside protocolized, aggressive supportive care. Every patient received remdesivir, administered intravenously with an initial loading dose of 200 milligrams followed by maintenance doses, typically 100 milligrams daily for total treatment durations ranging up to ten days. In one instance, the 15-year-old female received a maintenance regimen of 100 milligrams twice daily for seven days. For the 35-year-old patient who developed an aspartate aminotransferase level of 1,153 units per liter and an alanine aminotransferase level of 596 units per liter, clinicians temporarily suspended remdesivir after five days due to concern over drug-induced hepatic stress. Following a five-day therapeutic interruption and subsequent biochemical improvement in liver function, remdesivir was safely re-administered for five additional daily doses, achieving a completed 10-day course without recurrence of severe transaminitis. Supportive interventions targeted fluid homeostasis, symptomatic relief, and hemostatic stabilization tailored to individual clinical severity and local resources. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation using crystalloid fluids and dextrose-containing solutions was deployed to counteract ongoing gastrointestinal losses from vomiting and profuse diarrhea. For patients exhibiting active gastrointestinal hemorrhage, clinical teams administered intravenous tranexamic acid to support hemostatic control, supplemented by vitamin K, fresh-frozen plasma, intravenous omeprazole for gastrointestinal mucosal protection, and metoclopramide for symptom management. Broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics, including ceftriaxone combined with metronidazole or intravenous meropenem, were administered to selected patients exhibiting profound neutropenia or suspected secondary bacterial infections, in line with national management guidance. Virological monitoring via serial reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction assays confirmed progressive viral clearance across the cohort. In the infected healthcare worker, serial cycle threshold values rose steadily from 20.8 at admission to 25.4, 29, and 35, reflecting a diminishing viral burden before achieving an initial negative molecular test on day 12 and confirmatory clearance on day 14. Across all five survivors, viral clearance—verified by two consecutive negative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction tests performed within a 48-hour window—was successfully achieved between days 6 and 12 of treatment. All five patients achieved complete clinical recovery and resolution of laboratory abnormalities, and were subsequently discharged in stable condition after hospital stays spanning 10 to 14 days. When placed in the broader context of the regional outbreak, treatment timing appeared to be a notable distinguishing factor between survivors and non-survivors. Out of the 14 laboratory-confirmed outbreak cases, ten individuals received remdesivir while four received supportive care alone; all four patients who did not receive the antiviral agent died. Among the ten patients who were administered remdesivir, the five survivors presented early in their clinical illness and received timely interventions, whereas five patients who presented at an advanced, delayed stage of disease succumbed despite receiving antiviral therapy. The authors note, however, that because these observations originate from an emergency outbreak response with a small sample size and no control for baseline illness severity, they cannot establish a definitive causal link between remdesivir and survival, emphasizing the need for continued prospective clinical trials. The study authors conclude that dynamic monitoring of hepatic function and viral clearance is essential when delivering supportive care and experimental antivirals in resource-constrained environments. Although standard approved treatments and vaccines for Marburg virus remain unavailable, the successful recovery of all five patients demonstrates that filovirus infections are not uniformly fatal, even when complicated by profound cytopenias and acute gastrointestinal hemorrhage. The clinical course of these cases highlights the crucial importance of early case detection, immediate presentation to specialized treatment facilities, and structured hemodynamic and supportive management, while underscoring the urgent necessity of rigorous infection prevention and personal protective equipment adherence to interrupt transmission chains in both healthcare and domestic settings. Highlights Island Pharmaceuticals' antiviral Galidesivir has demonstrated 94 per cent survival in Marburg non-human primate models, supporting its advancement under the FDA's Animal Rule pathway. A blinded dose-response study is set to commence in December 2026, with survival results expected within weeks of the observation period closing. The FDA has confirmed that Galidesivir qualifies for a Tropical Disease Priority Review Voucher upon approval — with recent PRV sales setting a substantial market reference point. Uganda government approvals have been secured to evaluate Galidesivir in an active Ebola outbreak under the WHO MEURI framework, providing a unique human data generation opportunity. Island Pharmaceuticals Limited (ASX:ILA) is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on developing broad-acting antiviral therapies for infectious disease threats with limited or no approved treatments. The company's lead programme, Galidesivir, is an adenosine nucleoside analogue that works by blocking viral RNA polymerase replication and has demonstrated meaningful activity against more than 20 RNA viruses in preclinical settings, including filoviruses such as Marburg, Ebola, and Bundibugyo. The Marburg Opportunity and the Animal Rule Pathway Marburg virus represents the only Category A bioterrorism threat that currently has no approved treatment available in the United States Strategic National Stockpile. Its extremely high case fatality rate and history of interest from a bioterrorism perspective have made developing a countermeasure a persistent priority for public health agencies. The FDA's Animal Rule permits approval of medical countermeasures for diseases where human efficacy trials are not feasible or ethical, using controlled animal studies as the primary evidence for efficacy. This approach has successfully produced eight approved bioterrorism countermeasures since 2012, most of which have entered the Strategic National Stockpile under multi-year procurement contracts. Island Pharmaceuticals acquired Galidesivir from BioCryst in July 2025, following earlier development funded by US government research agencies. Within 15 months of that acquisition, the company progressed through manufacturing, regulatory engagement, and the commencement of non-human primate surgeries. The FDA has confirmed the Animal Rule pathway is appropriate for Marburg, provided Orphan Drug Designation, and confirmed that Galidesivir would qualify for a Tropical Disease Priority Review Voucher on approval — a designation with meaningful commercial value based on recent transactions. Near-Term Clinical Milestones and Uganda Programme The imminent dose-response study beginning in early December will evaluate different dosing levels in Marburg-infected primates to identify the optimal therapeutic dose and treatment window. Results are expected within weeks of the observation period closing. A second study assessing the time window for effective treatment initiation is scheduled to follow in early 2027, with the pivotal efficacy study expected to begin around mid-2027. The historical NHP survival data from prior work already shows compelling results, including 94 per cent survival when treatment commenced within 48 hours of infection — a treatment window that is clinically meaningful relative to real-world outbreak scenarios. In parallel with the animal programme, Island Pharmaceuticals has secured approvals from the Ugandan government and international health authorities to evaluate Galidesivir under the WHO's Monitored Emergency Use of Unregistered and Investigational Interventions framework in the context of the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the country. This represents the first opportunity to generate prospective human safety and efficacy data in a real outbreak setting, complementing the controlled animal studies and supporting a more comprehensive regulatory dossier. Key Insights Island Pharmaceuticals has assembled a clinical and regulatory framework for Galidesivir that combines an FDA-endorsed development pathway, meaningful historical efficacy data, and a rare opportunity for real-world human data generation in Uganda. The key near-term catalysts are the blinded dose-response NHP study results and the Uganda MEURI programme's initial patient data. Successful outcomes in both could substantially de-risk the path to a pivotal study and, ultimately, a regulatory filing. The potential for a Priority Review Voucher adds a commercial dimension that could attract Partnership interest well before approval. Questions and Answers FAQs Q: What is Galidesivir? A: Galidesivir is a broad-spectrum antiviral compound that blocks viral RNA polymerase replication and has demonstrated activity against more than 20 RNA viruses, including Marburg, Ebola, Zika, and Nipah. Q: What is the FDA Animal Rule? A: It is a regulatory pathway that allows the FDA to approve medical countermeasures for life-threatening conditions where human efficacy trials are not feasible, using animal model data to support an efficacy finding. Q: What is a Priority Review Voucher? A: A Priority Review Voucher (PRV) is a transferable certificate awarded by the FDA upon approval of a drug for a tropical or rare paediatric disease. It can be used or sold to accelerate the review of another drug. Q: What is the MEURI framework? A: The WHO's Monitored Emergency Use of Unregistered and Investigational Interventions framework allows investigational medicines to be used in outbreak situations where no approved treatment exists, with prospective data collection. Q: What are the next key milestones for Island Pharmaceuticals? A: The dose-response NHP study commencing in early December 2026, with results expected before the end of the year; a second NHP study in early 2027 to assess treatment timing; and the initiation of human data collection under the Uganda MEURI programme. Highlights Island Pharmaceuticals' antiviral Galidesivir has demonstrated 94 per cent survival in Marburg non-human primate models, supporting its advancement under the FDA's Animal Rule pathway. A blinded dose-response study is set to commence in December 2026, with survival results expected within weeks of the observation period closing. The FDA has confirmed that Galidesivir qualifies for a Tropical Disease Priority Review Voucher upon approval — with recent PRV sales setting a substantial market reference point. Uganda government approvals have been secured to evaluate Galidesivir in an active Ebola outbreak under the WHO MEURI framework, providing a unique human data generation opportunity. Island Pharmaceuticals Limited (ASX:ILA) is a clinical-stage biotechnology company focused on developing broad-acting antiviral therapies for infectious disease threats with limited or no approved treatments. The company's lead programme, Galidesivir, is an adenosine nucleoside analogue that works by blocking viral RNA polymerase replication and has demonstrated meaningful activity against more than 20 RNA viruses in preclinical settings, including filoviruses such as Marburg, Ebola, and Bundibugyo. The Marburg Opportunity and the Animal Rule Pathway Marburg virus represents the only Category A bioterrorism threat that currently has no approved treatment available in the United States Strategic National Stockpile. Its extremely high case fatality rate and history of interest from a bioterrorism perspective have made developing a countermeasure a persistent priority for public health agencies. The FDA's Animal Rule permits approval of medical countermeasures for diseases where human efficacy trials are not feasible or ethical, using controlled animal studies as the primary evidence for efficacy. This approach has successfully produced eight approved bioterrorism countermeasures since 2012, most of which have entered the Strategic National Stockpile under multi-year procurement contracts. Island Pharmaceuticals acquired Galidesivir from BioCryst in July 2025, following earlier development funded by US government research agencies. Within 15 months of that acquisition, the company progressed through manufacturing, regulatory engagement, and the commencement of non-human primate surgeries. The FDA has confirmed the Animal Rule pathway is appropriate for Marburg, provided Orphan Drug Designation, and confirmed that Galidesivir would qualify for a Tropical Disease Priority Review Voucher on approval — a designation with meaningful commercial value based on recent transactions. Near-Term Clinical Milestones and Uganda Programme The imminent dose-response study beginning in early December will evaluate different dosing levels in Marburg-infected primates to identify the optimal therapeutic dose and treatment window. Results are expected within weeks of the observation period closing. A second study assessing the time window for effective treatment initiation is scheduled to follow in early 2027, with the pivotal efficacy study expected to begin around mid-2027. A: Galidesivir is a broad-spectrum antiviral compound that blocks viral RNA polymerase replication and has demonstrated activity against more than 20 RNA viruses, including Marburg, Ebola, Zika, and Nipah. Q: What is the FDA Animal Rule? A: It is a regulatory pathway that allows the FDA to approve medical countermeasures for life-threatening conditions where human efficacy trials are not feasible, using animal model data to support an efficacy finding. Q: What is a Priority Review Voucher? A: A Priority Review Voucher (PRV) is a transferable certificate awarded by the FDA upon approval of a drug for a tropical or rare paediatric disease. A: The WHO's Monitored Emergency Use of Unregistered and Investigational Interventions framework allows investigational medicines to be used in outbreak situations where no approved treatment exists, with prospective data collection. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, November 23, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Five Marburg Virus Patients Recovered Following Early Antiviral and Supportive Care by November 19, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Five Marburg Virus Patients Recovered Following Early Antiviral and Supportive Care Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A detailed clinical case series documenting five laboratory-confirmed survivors of Marburg virus disease in southern Ethiopia indicates that early diagnostic identification paired with prompt antiviral administration and supportive care can achieve viral clearance and full clinical recovery, even when individuals present with severe gastrointestinal hemorrhage or significant hepatic injury. The findings, published in the International Journal of Emergency Medicine, examine patients treated at the Jinka General Hospital Marburg Virus Disease Treatment Center during an outbreak declared by the Ethiopian Ministry of Health in late October 2025. Across the entire outbreak response, public health surveillance identified 19 total cases, comprising 14 laboratory-confirmed infections and five probable cases. Among the 14 confirmed cases, nine individuals died, reflecting an overall case fatality rate of 64.3 percent, while five survived following intensive inpatient management. Marburg virus disease is a severe, often lethal hemorrhagic fever caused by Marburg virus, a member of the Filoviridae family first identified in 1967 after simultaneous outbreaks in Marburg and Frankfurt, Germany, and Belgrade, Yugoslavia, linked to laboratory work with African green monkeys imported from Uganda. The pathogen maintains a natural wildlife reservoir in the Egyptian fruit bat, and human infections carry historical case fatality rates ranging between 24 percent and 90 percent depending on the specific viral strain, host factors, and local clinical capabilities. Clinically, the infection typically begins with an abrupt, nonspecific febrile illness characterized by high fever, severe headache, chills, and profound fatigue, before progressing rapidly to severe gastrointestinal manifestations such as intractable vomiting, profuse watery diarrhea, and intense abdominal pain. Advanced stages frequently involve coagulation abnormalities, marked vascular permeability, and overt bleeding, which can precipitate multi-organ failure, circulatory collapse, and shock. The five survivors detailed in the report included four females and one male with a median age of 18 years, who were admitted and managed between November and December 2025. Epidemiological evaluations revealed that four of the cases arose through identifiable transmission chains within community and occupational settings. Three patients were household contacts of known probable or confirmed Marburg cases, including one individual whose father was a probable case and whose uncle died of confirmed disease, and another patient who provided extensive caregiver support to two infected siblings who both died. A fourth patient was a 32-year-old female healthcare worker stationed at the Jinka treatment center who had direct occupational contact with confirmed patients over a two-week period and later served in pre-triage care, where she assisted during the delivery-related care of an infected woman despite wearing personal protective equipment. Upon hospital admission, all five patients exhibited classic initial clinical manifestations of filovirus infection, presenting uniformly with fever, generalized headache, fatigue, and gastrointestinal complaints. Hematological and biochemical evaluations across the cohort demonstrated classic hallmarks of systemic filoviral illness, including profound bone marrow suppression and direct hepatocellular injury. Marked leukopenia was documented across the cohort, reaching a nadir white blood cell count of 1.55 times 10 to the third power cells per microliter, accompanied by severe thrombocytopenia with a platelet nadir of 65 times 10 to the third power cells per microliter. Hepatic involvement was universally evident through elevated transaminases, reaching an extreme peak aspartate aminotransferase level of 1,153 units per liter in one severely affected patient. Additionally, one patient experienced profound neutropenia, with an absolute neutrophil count dropping to 107 cells per microliter. Overt hemorrhagic complications developed in three of the five survivors between the fifth and seventh days after symptom onset, a timeline that mirrors the progression seen in previous Central and East African outbreaks. The first patient, a 15-year-old female who presented five days after contact with a suspected fatal case, suffered three episodes of hematemesis alongside high fever, cough, abdominal pain, and scattered erythematous maculopapular skin lesions. Another patient, an 18-year-old female admitted shortly after the death of a suspected household contact, quickly progressed into the hemorrhagic phase, experiencing significant upper gastrointestinal bleeding with baseline hemoglobin measurements fluctuating between 11.6 and 14.6 grams per deciliter. A 35-year-old female caregiver similarly presented with bloody diarrhea and a history of upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage, followed by a critical phase around day five marked by persistent fever reaching 39.5 degrees Celsius and severe hepatic injury. Therapeutic management for all five surviving patients integrated experimental antiviral therapy alongside protocolized, aggressive supportive care. Every patient received remdesivir, administered intravenously with an initial loading dose of 200 milligrams followed by maintenance doses, typically 100 milligrams daily for total treatment durations ranging up to ten days. In one instance, the 15-year-old female received a maintenance regimen of 100 milligrams twice daily for seven days. For the 35-year-old patient who developed an aspartate aminotransferase level of 1,153 units per liter and an alanine aminotransferase level of 596 units per liter, clinicians temporarily suspended remdesivir after five days due to concern over drug-induced hepatic stress. Following a five-day therapeutic interruption and subsequent biochemical improvement in liver function, remdesivir was safely re-administered for five additional daily doses, achieving a completed 10-day course without recurrence of severe transaminitis. Supportive interventions targeted fluid homeostasis, symptomatic relief, and hemostatic stabilization tailored to individual clinical severity and local resources. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation using crystalloid fluids and dextrose-containing solutions was deployed to counteract ongoing gastrointestinal losses from vomiting and profuse diarrhea. For patients exhibiting active gastrointestinal hemorrhage, clinical teams administered intravenous tranexamic acid to support hemostatic control, supplemented by vitamin K, fresh-frozen plasma, intravenous omeprazole for gastrointestinal mucosal protection, and metoclopramide for symptom management. Broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics, including ceftriaxone combined with metronidazole or intravenous meropenem, were administered to selected patients exhibiting profound neutropenia or suspected secondary bacterial infections, in line with national management guidance. Virological monitoring via serial reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction assays confirmed progressive viral clearance across the cohort. In the infected healthcare worker, serial cycle threshold values rose steadily from 20.8 at admission to 25.4, 29, and 35, reflecting a diminishing viral burden before achieving an initial negative molecular test on day 12 and confirmatory clearance on day 14. Across all five survivors, viral clearance—verified by two consecutive negative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction tests performed within a 48-hour window—was successfully achieved between days 6 and 12 of treatment. All five patients achieved complete clinical recovery and resolution of laboratory abnormalities, and were subsequently discharged in stable condition after hospital stays spanning 10 to 14 days. When placed in the broader context of the regional outbreak, treatment timing appeared to be a notable distinguishing factor between survivors and non-survivors. Out of the 14 laboratory-confirmed outbreak cases, ten individuals received remdesivir while four received supportive care alone; all four patients who did not receive the antiviral agent died. Among the ten patients who were administered remdesivir, the five survivors presented early in their clinical illness and received timely interventions, whereas five patients who presented at an advanced, delayed stage of disease succumbed despite receiving antiviral therapy. The authors note, however, that because these observations originate from an emergency outbreak response with a small sample size and no control for baseline illness severity, they cannot establish a definitive causal link between remdesivir and survival, emphasizing the need for continued prospective clinical trials. The study authors conclude that dynamic monitoring of hepatic function and viral clearance is essential when delivering supportive care and experimental antivirals in resource-constrained environments. Although standard approved treatments and vaccines for Marburg virus remain unavailable, the successful recovery of all five patients demonstrates that filovirus infections are not uniformly fatal, even when complicated by profound cytopenias and acute gastrointestinal hemorrhage. The clinical course of these cases highlights the crucial importance of early case detection, immediate presentation to specialized treatment facilities, and structured hemodynamic and supportive management, while underscoring the urgent necessity of rigorous infection prevention and personal protective equipment adherence to interrupt transmission chains in both healthcare and domestic settings.
